question: How can a repeated dance rhythm remain clear while its harmony keeps changing?
intro: The Forlane sets a dotted dance rhythm against harmonies that resist settling into simple triads. This selection combines different pianists and omits the fourth movement, the Rigaudon; it is not a complete performance of the suite.

sections.label: Dotted dance and repeated strains
sections.mNote: The dance rhythm persists through short, repeated phrases.

sections.label: Middle contrasts
sections.mNote: Chordal accents and sustained lines change the dance’s weight.

sections.label: Later dance figures
sections.mNote: Familiar rhythmic figures take different harmonic routes.

sections.label: Closing gestures
sections.mNote: Soft, separated gestures end without a written slowing.

cues.title: Unequal steps in six
cues.text: The dance is in 6/8, but its dotted notes make the steps unequal. Keep the two broad beats in mind while listening to the long–short figures inside them. The rhythm is more regular than the harmonies laid over it.
cues.evidence: Durand 1918 piano score, printed p. 10: Allegretto, 6/8, dotted quaver–semiquaver figures and chromatically altered chords. This describes the opening rhythm, not a measured tempo.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Remembering Gabriel Deluc
cues.text: The score dedicates the Forlane to Lieutenant Gabriel Deluc, a Basque painter and friend of Ravel who was killed in the First World War. His name stands over an old dance form, not a movement labelled as a lament.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 10, and BnF dedication list: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Kansas City Symphony programme, printed pp. 5–6, identifies Deluc as a Basque painter and records the memorial context: https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf.

cues.title: A quieter hinge
cues.text: The volume drops in this passage, but the dance’s uneven step remains available to the ear. Follow the rhythm through the quieter notes rather than mistaking a smaller dynamic for a slower tempo.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/ravel-tombeau-forlane.txt: loudness falls from −11.1 dB at 65 seconds to −17.0 at 70, with boundary candidates at 70 and 74. The measurement establishes a local reduction in level, not a tempo change.

cues.title: Melody inside the chords
cues.text: A chord need not move as one block. Ravel often holds one note while a neighbouring voice shifts by a small interval. Listen for those inner movements: they make the harmony restless even when the dance rhythm remains easy to recognise.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 10–12, ties and independent voice-leading within the chordal texture. This is a passage-level listening task; no particular inner note or chord change is assigned to 105 seconds.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An older dance studied
cues.text: The forlane began as a northern Italian dance and entered French courtly music. Ravel studied the tradition directly: he transcribed the forlane from Couperin’s fourth Concert royal. His own movement preserves a recognisable dance rhythm while giving it much less predictable chords.
cues.evidence: Kansas City Symphony programme, printed pp. 6–7, documents the dance’s route into France and Ravel’s transcription of Couperin’s forlane: https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf. Ravel’s score supplies the rhythmic and harmonic comparison.

cues.title: Accents without a new dance
cues.text: The middle pages vary the weight of the writing: detached chords, linked melodic notes and a bass that does not always attack with the upper part. Listen for the resulting changes of emphasis without losing the underlying two-beat sway.
cues.evidence: Durand score, printed pp. 12–13, contrasts detached chordal attacks with tied lower voices and slurred melodic figures. The section marker is an approximate middle-passage division; the score’s 6/8 metre continues.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Less volume, more detail
cues.text: This central stretch is quieter than many of the surrounding dance phrases. Use the smaller dynamic to listen into the chord: distinguish a note that continues sounding from a newly struck note beside it.
cues.evidence: Analysis windows at 200–245 seconds range roughly from −12.9 to −19.3 dB, below the −8 to −11 dB levels frequent earlier. The score’s tied voices motivate the listening task; the report does not identify individual pitches.

cues.title: Finishing away from the front
cues.text: After wartime service and illness, Ravel recovered in Normandy and completed the piano suite in November 1917. Its repeated strains and neatly balanced phrases were worked out amid the interruption of his own career, not in an untouched eighteenth-century retreat.
cues.evidence: Kansas City Symphony programme, printed pp. 5–6, documents the Normandy recovery and completion; BnF dates completion November 1917. The contrast is historical context, not an interpretation of this passage as autobiography.

cues.title: The dance gains weight
cues.text: The quieter central stretch gives way to a stronger dynamic. Notice how much can change without replacing the dance rhythm: a firmer bass and more emphatic chords can enlarge the same kind of long–short movement.
cues.evidence: Analysis rises from −15.7 dB at 270 seconds to −10.7 at 275, −9.7 at 280 and −8.7 at 290. The cue identifies a dynamic expansion; it does not use this measurement to assert an exact refrain return.

cues.title: Recognition without exact repetition
cues.text: The score repeatedly brings back the dance’s characteristic figures, but changes their surroundings. Listen for a rhythm you recognise before trying to identify the chord beneath it. Familiar gestures can lead somewhere different when the bass or an inner note changes.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 14–15, reworks dotted figures and falling melodic shapes with altered bass notes and inner voices. The overall rondo character is described in the Kansas City Symphony programme, p. 7; no exact formal return is timed here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Decoration within the phrase
cues.text: Trills and small-note ornaments interrupt the surface without replacing the phrase. Try hearing through them to the sustained melody underneath. In this score, as in the Prélude, the grace notes are placed on the beat rather than hurried in before it.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 15, trills and small-note ornaments; p. 10 footnote instructs that small notes are struck on the beat. This cue concerns the later passage as a whole, not a particular trill onset.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Softly, without slowing
cues.text: The ending thins out and becomes quieter. Ravel writes “sans ralentir” — without slowing — over the final gesture. Listen for the difference between fewer attacks and a slower underlying pulse: silence between notes need not mean the dance has changed speed.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 15, final pp and “sans ralentir”. Analysis falls from −11.7 dB at 390 seconds to −17.4 at 395 and −32.0 at 410, while attack density decreases. No measured tempo claim is made.

transitions.title: The rhythm outlasts the texture
transitions.how: The dotted dance figure links phrases with different kinds of accompaniment. Ravel shifts between detached chordal attacks and notes sustained across the beat; the piano’s bass and upper voices need not move together. The continuity lies in the 6/8 dance rhythm, not in a single unchanging chord pattern.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 12–13, contrasts chordal and sustained textures within 6/8. The recording analysis has a strong boundary candidate at 170 seconds. It supports a broad listening division, not a bar-aligned formal episode boundary.

transitions.title: Familiar figures, altered surroundings
transitions.how: A local reduction in force lets the rhythmic detail emerge again. The later score keeps recognisable dotted figures and ornaments while altering the bass and the notes held inside the chords. The join is carried by that shared vocabulary; it is not a restart of the entire opening.
transitions.evidence: Analysis has a boundary candidate at 300 seconds; loudness falls from −11.8 dB at 295 to −18.9 at 300 before recovering. Durand score, pp. 14–15, supplies the description of reworked figures. No exact rondo-return boundary is claimed.

transitions.title: The dance leaves space
transitions.how: Ravel reduces the ending to short gestures, held notes and rests. The softer dynamic and fewer attacks release the accumulated activity, but the final instruction explicitly resists slowing the pulse. The pianist must make a close without turning it into a large romantic ritardando.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 15, final rests, pp and “sans ralentir”. Analysis boundary candidate at 394 seconds; level and attack density fall over the final twenty seconds.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
